question:
For natural numbers k and i with 0 <= i <= k, work over the real polynomial ring and define B_{d,r}(t)=C(d,r)*t^r*(1-t)^(d-r) for 0 <= r <= d. The predecessor described the endpoint-factor term t^i*(1-t)^(k+1) as having degree k+1. Is this true for every allowed i? Determine its exact degree and leading coefficient, give a counterexample to the universal description if false, and distinguish that degree from the Bernstein representation degree d=2*k+1.

Prove, for every real t, the exact identity t^i*(1-t)^(k+1)=sum_{j=0}^{k-i} w(k,i,j)*B_{d,i+j}(t), where w(k,i,j)=C(k-i,j)/C(d,i+j), with the binomial coefficients regarded as real numbers. Justify the nonzero denominators and handle i=0, i=k and k=0 without assuming t is strictly between the endpoints.

To make the same full source polynomial explicit, set a_{k,i}=sum_{m=0}^{i} C(k+i-m,k)/m! for 0 <= i <= k, F_k(t)=(1-t)^(k+1)*sum_{i=0}^{k} a_{k,i}*t^i, and H_k(t)=exp(-1)*F_k(t)+F_k(1-t). Thus H_k(t) is the source interpolant evaluated at p=t-1. Give a degree-d Bernstein coefficient formula for H_k by collecting the elevated terms and reflecting their indices. Prove its coefficients are nonnegative real numbers, and deduce H_k(t)>=0 on [0,1]. Separate the all-real exact identity from the interval restriction used for nonnegativity of the basis functions.
reference_answer:
The predecessor's universal degree description is false. The factor (1-t)^(k+1) has leading term (-1)^(k+1)*t^(k+1); multiplying by t^i gives the nonzero leading coefficient (-1)^(k+1) at degree i+k+1. This equals k+1 exactly when i=0. For k=i=1 the term is t*(1-t)^2=t-2*t^2+t^3, of degree3 rather than2. Since i<=k, its actual degree is at most d=2*k+1, reaching d when i=k. The degree-d Bernstein basis is an ambient representation choice, not an assertion that every term has exact degree d. These terms are never zero or constant polynomials, since k+1>=1 and their leading coefficients are nonzero.

For 0<=j<=k-i we have 0<=i+j<=k<=d, hence C(d,i+j)>0 and its real reciprocal is defined. Multiplication cancels that binomial factor in w*B. The exponent relation d-(i+j)=(k+1)+(k-i-j) then gives
w(k,i,j)*B_{d,i+j}(t)=t^i*(1-t)^(k+1)*C(k-i,j)*t^j*(1-t)^(k-i-j).
Summing over j yields the fixed endpoint term multiplied by (t+(1-t))^(k-i)=1, by the binomial theorem. This proves the polynomial identity, hence its evaluation at every real t; no division by t or 1-t occurs. For i=k the sum has only j=0 and gives w=1/C(d,k), with no increase in actual degree. For i=0 it is the usual expansion of (1-t)^(k+1) into this ambient basis. For k=0 necessarily i=j=0 and the identity is B_{1,0}(t)=1-t. At t=0 or1 the same polynomial evaluations remain valid, using the standard constant-polynomial convention t^0=1, including 0^0=1 in such evaluations.

Each a_{k,i} is nonnegative, because every binomial numerator is nonnegative and m! is a positive real number. For r=0,...,d define
L_{k,r}=sum_{i=0}^{k} sum_{j=0}^{k-i} [r=i+j]*a_{k,i}*w(k,i,j),
where the bracket is1 when the index equality holds and0 otherwise. Finite collection of the exact single-term identities gives F_k(t)=sum_{r=0}^{d} L_{k,r}*B_{d,r}(t). All L_{k,r} are nonnegative, and L_{k,r}=0 for r>k. The reflection identity B_{d,r}(1-t)=B_{d,d-r}(t) gives F_k(1-t)=sum_{r=0}^{d} L_{k,d-r}*B_{d,r}(t). Therefore
H_k(t)=sum_{r=0}^{d} c_{k,r}*B_{d,r}(t), with c_{k,r}=exp(-1)*L_{k,r}+L_{k,d-r}>=0.
The positive exponential weight multiplies the unreflected F_k, exactly as in the source formula; it is not moved to the other endpoint. This is the degree-d coefficient vector for the same H_k. Its nonnegativity is a statement about real coefficients, independent of t. On [0,1] the powers in every B_{d,r} are nonnegative, so the displayed sum implies H_k(t)>=0. The coefficient positivity alone makes no claim about signs of the basis outside that interval. At k=0 the coefficients are exp(-1) and1 and H_0(t)=exp(-1)*(1-t)+t, consistent with all formulas.
